# Mixed effect model

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results=FALSE, output=FALSE}
#Load library so functions run smoothly
library(tidyverse)
```

![](images/mixtape.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"}

In the last example we had one outcome variable (e.g. E.coli abundance) and one predictor variable (e.g. drug dose).
In real life we will commonly have more than one predictor variable in our experiments.
Thankfully, linear regression can have three or more variables.

Once you start using more variables they can start to interact with each other in various ways.
This is when Mixed Effect Modelling, also known as Hierarchical modelling, can be useful.
This is important for us to know as MaAsLin3 stands for **Microbiome Multivariable Associations with Linear Models** and uses Mixed effect linear models.

In simplest terms, a mixed effect model is when you have multiple linear regressions for your data based on different nested groups.
To explain this further we'll go through the following concepts:

- Nested data
- Random intercept
- Random slope
- Random slope + intercept

## Nested data

Nested data is when your observations are within groups. This could be:

- Age groups
- Demographics
- Gender
- Experimental blocks
- Sequencing runs

Let's look at a concrete example with our _E.coli_ data from the last page.
However, in this case we have more datapoints.
Our original data was 75 patients from hospital 1 (H1).
Our new set of 75 patients are from hospital 2 (H2).
These two sets of patients are our two nested groups.

:::{.callout-note}
You can have a lot more than just 2 nested groups.
:::

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results=FALSE}
set.seed(222)
Dosage <- c(sample(10:100,25), sample(100:500,25), sample(500:1000,25), 
            sample(10:100,25), sample(100:750,25), sample(500:1000,25))
Ecoli <- c(sample(75:150,25), sample(80:180,25), sample(100:250,25), 
            sample(50:100,25), sample(20:80,25), sample(1:40,25))
Ecoli <- Ecoli/10
#Nest by hospital
Hospital <- c(rep(x = "H1", times = 75), rep(x = "H2", times = 75))
#Tibble
tbl <- tibble::tibble(Dosage, Ecoli, Hospital)
set.seed(NULL)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results=FALSE}
#linear rgession
#Calculate linear model
ecoli_lm <- lm(Ecoli ~ Dosage, data = tbl)
#Intercept and gradient
c <- ecoli_lm$coefficients[1]
m <- ecoli_lm$coefficients[2]
#equation
lm_equation <- stringr::str_c(
    "y = ", as.character(round(m, digits=5)),"x + ",as.character(round(c,digits=2))
)
#plot
tbl |>
    ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x=Dosage, y=Ecoli)) +
    ggplot2::geom_smooth(method='lm', formula= y~x) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(aes(color=Hospital)) +
    ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 100, y = 22, label = lm_equation) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "Antibiotic dosage (mg/kg)", y = "E.coli relative abundance (%)")
```

In this case we can see that our simple linear model based only on _E.coli_ abundance and Antibiotic dosage is not fit for purpose.

## Random intercepts

The first addition to our linear model to incorporate mixed effects is to add random intercepts.
In essence this is allowing each group to have different intercept values.


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Random?"}
The word "random" can be confusing, here. 
The intercepts are not chosen randomly. 
Instead A random intercept allows each group to have its own baseline (intercept) value rather than sharing the same one across groups.

In our example samples from different hospitals start from slightly different average E. coli abundances. 
The model estimates these hospital-specific baselines, while also estimating the overall average across all hospitals. 
This means each hospital can differ, but the model still tries to learn what is typical across hospitals.
:::

Let's see that in practice with our dataset.

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results=FALSE}
#filter tbl
h1_tbl <- tbl |> dplyr::filter(Hospital=="H1")
h2_tbl <- tbl |> dplyr::filter(Hospital=="H2")
#linear regressions
#Calculate linear model
ecoli_lm <- lm(Ecoli ~ Dosage, data = tbl)
#Intercept and gradient
c <- ecoli_lm$coefficients[1]
m <- ecoli_lm$coefficients[2]
#Hospital 1 linear model
h1_lm <- lm(Ecoli ~ Dosage, data = h1_tbl)
#Intercept and gradient
h1_c <- h1_lm$coefficients[1]
h1_m <- h1_lm$coefficients[2]
#AMR Calculate linear model
h2_lm <- lm(Ecoli ~ Dosage, data = h2_tbl)
#Intercept and gradient
h2_c <- h2_lm$coefficients[1]
h2_m <- h2_lm$coefficients[2]
#equation
h1_lm_equation <- stringr::str_c(
    "y = ", as.character(round(m, digits=5)),"x + ",as.character(round(h1_c,digits=2))
)
h2_lm_equation <- stringr::str_c(
    "y = ", as.character(round(m, digits=5)),"x + ",as.character(round(h1_c,digits=2))
)
#plot
tbl |>  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x=Dosage, y=Ecoli)) +
    ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = m, intercept = h1_c, color = "#f8766d", size=1) +
    ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = m, intercept=h2_c, color = "#00bfc4", size = 1) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(aes(color=Hospital)) +
    ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 250, y = 18.5, label = h1_lm_equation) +
    ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 875, y = 6, label = h2_lm_equation) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "Antibiotic dosage (mg/kg)", y = "E.coli relative abundance (%)")
```

The linear models for each nested group (Hospital 1 & 2) now start in good places since they have different intercepts.
However, they both have the same slope which does not fit either group very well.

## Random slope

Instead of random intercepts lets use random slopes.
This gives each group its own slope.

Below is our data with random slopes but the same intercept.

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results=FALSE}
#filter tbl
h1_tbl <- tbl |> dplyr::filter(Hospital=="H1")
h2_tbl <- tbl |> dplyr::filter(Hospital=="H2")
#linear regressions
#Calculate linear model
ecoli_lm <- lm(Ecoli ~ Dosage, data = tbl)
#Intercept and gradient
c <- ecoli_lm$coefficients[1]
m <- ecoli_lm$coefficients[2]
#Hospital 1 linear model
h1_lm <- lm(Ecoli ~ Dosage, data = h1_tbl)
#Intercept and gradient
h1_c <- h1_lm$coefficients[1]
h1_m <- h1_lm$coefficients[2]
#AMR Calculate linear model
h2_lm <- lm(Ecoli ~ Dosage, data = h2_tbl)
#Intercept and gradient
h2_c <- h2_lm$coefficients[1]
h2_m <- h2_lm$coefficients[2]
#equation
h1_lm_equation <- stringr::str_c(
    "y = ", as.character(round(m, digits=5)),"x + ",as.character(round(h1_c,digits=2))
)
h2_lm_equation <- stringr::str_c(
    "y = ", as.character(round(m, digits=5)),"x + ",as.character(round(h1_c,digits=2))
)
#plot
tbl |>  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x=Dosage, y=Ecoli)) +
    ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = h1_m, intercept = c, color = "#f8766d", size=1) +
    ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = h2_m, intercept=c, color = "#00bfc4", size = 1) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(aes(color=Hospital)) +
    ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 250, y = 18.5, label = h1_lm_equation) +
    ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 875, y = 6, label = h2_lm_equation) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "Antibiotic dosage (mg/kg)", y = "E.coli relative abundance (%)")
```

This looks better but its still not perfect.

## Random slope and intercept

In mixed effect models both random slopes and random intercepts are can be used.
This allows you to best account for the differences between the groups.

Below is our final plot with random slopes and random intercepts.

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results=FALSE}
#filter tbl
h1_tbl <- tbl |> dplyr::filter(Hospital=="H1")
h2_tbl <- tbl |> dplyr::filter(Hospital=="H2")
#linear regressions
#Calculate linear model
ecoli_lm <- lm(Ecoli ~ Dosage, data = tbl)
#Intercept and gradient
c <- ecoli_lm$coefficients[1]
m <- ecoli_lm$coefficients[2]
#Hospital 1 linear model
h1_lm <- lm(Ecoli ~ Dosage, data = h1_tbl)
#Intercept and gradient
h1_c <- h1_lm$coefficients[1]
h1_m <- h1_lm$coefficients[2]
#AMR Calculate linear model
h2_lm <- lm(Ecoli ~ Dosage, data = h2_tbl)
#Intercept and gradient
h2_c <- h2_lm$coefficients[1]
h2_m <- h2_lm$coefficients[2]
#equation
h1_lm_equation <- stringr::str_c(
    "y = ", as.character(round(m, digits=5)),"x + ",as.character(round(h1_c,digits=2))
)
h2_lm_equation <- stringr::str_c(
    "y = ", as.character(round(m, digits=5)),"x + ",as.character(round(h1_c,digits=2))
)
#plot
tbl |>  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x=Dosage, y=Ecoli)) +
    ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = h1_m, intercept = h1_c, color = "#f8766d", size=1) +
    ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = h2_m, intercept=h2_c, color = "#00bfc4", size = 1) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(aes(color=Hospital)) +
    ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 250, y = 18.5, label = h1_lm_equation) +
    ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 875, y = 6, label = h2_lm_equation) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "Antibiotic dosage (mg/kg)", y = "E.coli relative abundance (%)")
```

For an animated explanation please see the following link: [mfviz Introduction to Hierarchical Modeling](https://mfviz.com/hierarchical-models/)

In our MaAsLin3 analysis we will only use random intercepts.
